newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Selling frenzy batters London copper market. [CORRECTED 18:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Selling frenzy batters London copper market. [CORRECTED 18:00 GMT]

text.p: A wave of speculative selling swept through the London Metal Exchange (LME) copper market on Wednesday, driving prices to the lowest levels for seven weeks.

The benchmark three months delivery price fell to $2,355 a tonne at one stage during hectic trading, down $82 from Tuesday (corrects from Monday). The beleaguered market is some $230, or nine percent, down from the $2,594 high of last Friday.
"I've no idea if there is anything behind the selling, other than the investment funds and option-related sales. I expect there was a bit of blood spilt on the floor today," one trader said.
"The market had been under pressure all morning but the late selling came from nowhere...once $2,400 was lost all hell broke loose," a floor trader said.
Analysts said the pull-back in copper prices was savage - only two weeks ago the market was riding high above $2,600 at its best since last June.
"There has been long liquidation, and maybe people are taking the view that there is only one way for it to go and that is down," Angus MacMillan of LME trader Billiton Metals said.

Some traders suggested a further small LME copper warehouse stocks rise this morning helped to dent a market that was already on the decline. Supply tightness, which gripped the market in the first half of 1997 is now relaxing in slow summer conditions.

As always, the decline was exaggerated and hastened by options activity. When prices fall option writers 'delta-hedge' by selling against put options that move into-the-money and unwinding cover against calls as these move out-of-the money.
"Between the $2,550 and $2,400 strikes (on July) the open interest is big enough so there is a 'double-whammy' when it goes down," one option trader said.

Lower prices are justified on a long-term fundamental basis, with copper supplies set to surge from monster mines in the Americas and the Far East, outpacing strong demand and resulting in surpluses in coming years.
But the short-term fundamentals tell a different story. "We still have nearby tightness and visible stocks are still at low levels," MacMillan said.
However, the copper downturn, like previous strong rallies, was not unusual for a market that is still working through the tail-stream of the Sumitomo affair.
Last June, the Japanese brokerage stunned the metals world with losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trading allegedly carried out by its former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka.
Hamanaka's legacy, on top of the losses, was a tangled web of off-market deals, complicated option strategies and mysterious inventory holdings.
"This particular market has been distorted for some time, and it is very difficult to know what positions might be out there," MacMillan said.
Given the extent and the speed of the fall, prices are probably oversold, so the market should now consolidate and bounce from the $2,350 line of support.
"It has done enough for the moment, and we would look to take some in down at these levels," a trader said.
Also, there is the day-to-day threat of the backwardation flaring out again. The cash/threes premium was near $150 on Tuesday, but contracted to near $110 on Wednesday.
The tightness is located from mid-July to the end of July. Yesterday the July/August backwardation was around $90, but now stands around $70.
"There are still people short of those dates. If they cover it (the backwardation) could shoot out again," the trader added.
--London Newsroom 44 171 542 8080
